title: {{NAME}} and the Game at the Edge of the Copper Hills
moral: The most useful thing you can offer someone who has never failed is the chance to fail safely, with a friend beside them.

pages.content:
The Copper Hills were named for their colour at sunset, which was exactly the warm amber-orange of old pennies, and they rose in gentle terraces above the valley where the robot settlement of Brackenmere had been built. Brackenmere was a village by robot standards, which meant it was meticulously organised and very quiet and had a football pitch of such mathematically precise dimensions that it had once been measured three times by three separate robots who had all arrived at the same answer and still wanted to be certain.

{{NAME}} arrived in Brackenmere on a Saturday afternoon when the pitch was occupied by a match in progress, a match so unusual in composition that he stopped on the hillside above the valley to watch it for a full minute before walking down.

One team was made up entirely of robots of various sizes and constructions, each moving with the careful, efficient grace of beings for whom coordination is a matter of calculation rather than instinct.

The other team was made up of unicorns.

The unicorns were winning, by a considerable margin, and this appeared to be causing the robots some complicated feelings. None of them showed distress in a way that was obvious. But there was a quality to their movements, a slight over-calculation, a hesitation between passing decisions, that in a human team would have been called rattled.

A small, bright-eyed robot in the referee's position noticed {{NAME}} on the hillside and raised one hand in a wave that was so precise it could have been used as a protractor.

pages.content:
The referee's name was 8-Spark, and it spoke in complete sentences delivered at the speed of someone who had decided that brevity was a form of respect.

The robot team was called the Brackenmere Gears. The unicorn team was passing through on a seasonal route that took them across the Copper Hills every year and had, five seasons ago, challenged the Gears to a friendly match, which had become an annual fixture partly because both sides enjoyed it and partly because neither side had yet managed to fully understand the other's approach to football.

'They play without communication,' 8-Spark explained, meaning the unicorns. 'No audible signals. No agreed patterns. They adjust in real time and their adjustments are always correct, because each of them processes the same information the same way simultaneously. We cannot do that. We each process differently.'

{{NAME}} watched the match carefully from the touchline. The unicorns' lead striker was a dun-coloured mare named Vesper who seemed to exist at the leading edge of every attacking move without anyone having discussed that she should be there.

The Gears' best player was a tall, angular robot called Long-Step, whose stride covered remarkable ground but who had a slight delay before each major decision, a visible processing pause that the unicorns had, very professionally, started to anticipate.

'Long-Step needs to decide before the moment,' {{NAME}} said. 'Not in it.'

8-Spark turned its bright sensor-eyes to him. 'That is what all the other coaches have said. We have not yet found out how.'

pages.content:
The second half began and {{NAME}} did something unexpected: he asked to play.

8-Spark consulted several things simultaneously before arriving at a yes, and {{NAME}} was slotted into the left side of midfield alongside Long-Step, who regarded him with sensor-eyes that cycled through amber and gold before settling on a welcoming green.

Playing with robots was, {{NAME}} discovered, extraordinary and disorienting in equal measure. The Gears never misjudged a pass. Every ball arrived where it should, on the correct foot, weighted perfectly. But they waited for each other to declare intentions before committing, a fraction of shared data exchange before every action, and that fraction was, against the telepathic fluency of the unicorns, the difference between good and excellent.

{{NAME}} played differently. He played on instinct, which meant he played on what he had already understood before the moment arrived, and Long-Step, watching him do this repeatedly from close range, began to do something new.

It began to predict him.

Not analyse. Predict. There was a difference, and Long-Step, being a robot who understood the difference between these things deeply and precisely, registered it.

The Gears scored twice in eleven minutes. Not by calculation. By {{NAME}} playing instinctively and Long-Step learning, at speed, to trust what {{NAME}}'s movement told it rather than waiting for declared data.

Vesper stopped mid-pitch after the second goal and looked at {{NAME}} with the specific approval of a competitor who has been made to work for something.

pages.content:
Three-three, last minute, and Long-Step broke through alone.

The robot ran with the mechanical perfection it always had, the ball guided forward with metronomic precision. The unicorn goalkeeper, a broad silver stallion named Birch, came out at an angle, moving on certainty.

Long-Step stopped.

Not a hesitation-stop. A thinking-stop. A stop that meant something.

Birch committed to the angle.

Long-Step waited one beat and went the other way, the kind of move that belongs to players who have understood not just where the keeper is but where the keeper has decided to be, which is a different and more sophisticated piece of information.

The ball went in.

The silence on the pitch was the sort that takes a moment to process. Then 8-Spark blew the final whistle and Long-Step did something none of the Gears had ever seen it do in five seasons of this fixture.

It raised both arms.

Not in the athlete's automatic triumph gesture. Deliberately. As if it had watched this gesture happen a hundred times from a distance and had been saving it for the right occasion.

Vesper trotted forward and pressed her nose briefly to Long-Step's extended hand. The gesture was gracious and equal and exactly right.

{{NAME}} sat down on the copper-coloured grass and laughed, from somewhere very deep and very satisfied, until his sides ached.

'What is funny?' Long-Step asked, looking down at him with its new green-sensor-eyes warmth.

'Nothing,' {{NAME}} said. 'Everything. All of it.'

pages.content:
The post-match gathering happened in Brackenmere's central square, which the robots had built to be exactly the right size for a town of their population and which happened to also be exactly the right size for a team of unicorns, which 8-Spark noted with the quiet satisfaction of something that had turned out better than designed.

Vesper stood beside {{NAME}} as the sun finished its work on the Copper Hills and the whole sky went to amber and rose.

She did not speak. Unicorns communicated through presence and gesture, and her presence was warm and companionable, which translated well enough.

{{NAME}} leaned against the town's central pillar, tired in the good way. Long-Step stood nearby, not exactly participating in the gathering, not exactly not participating, its sensor-eyes moving slowly between the various conversations as though cataloguing something about how this kind of evening worked.

8-Spark appeared at {{NAME}}'s elbow. 'Will you come next year?' it asked. 'For the fixture. We have held a place in the formation, provisionally. Left midfield, as before.'

{{NAME}} looked at Long-Step, at the unicorns dispersed through the amber square, at 8-Spark's bright patient sensor-eyes.

'Yes,' he said.

He was home and asleep before the copper hills had finished cooling, warm and still, and in the place just before sleep he heard, clearly and specifically, the sound of a ball struck perfectly, and a long mechanical stride covering the ground, and 8-Spark's whistle, which sounded tonight less like a signal and more like a song.
